title: TA9-08529
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXX (principal claimant) and XXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXX, citizens of Colombia, claim to be in need of refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1

The claims of their U.S. born sons, who are minors - XXXX XXXXX (TA9-08531) and XXXX XXXXX (TA9-08532) - were disjoined and rendered a separate bench negative decision. The principal claimant was appointed designated representative for the sons.
The principal claimant is a 30-year old man from Bogota, Colombia. He and his 30-year old wife married in the U.S. in 2006. The wife bases her claim on the principal claimant's story.

The principal claimant said that in 2000, he worked as a XXXX XXXX XXXX or XXXX to people accused in criminal cases in Bogota. In the course of his work, he was threatened by a FARC prisoner. Since then, he traveled back-and-forth to the U.S., as follows:2 * XXXX, 2000 - Left for the U.S., due to threats received on XXXX, 2000. * XXXX, 2000 - Returned to Bogota, "since no more threats were received." * XXXX, 2000 - Left for the U.S., no threats received. * Shortly after - Returned to Bogota. * XXXX, 2001 - Left for the U.S. after receiving threatening letter from FARC (Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia) 4 months earlier on XXXX, 2001. * XXXX, 2001 - Returned to Bogota. * XXXX, 2002 - Left for the U.S., after mother in Bogota received threat to the principal claimant. * XXXX, 2002 - Returned to Bogota, as he said "no more threats." Started studies at university in Bogota and opened a restaurant in Bogota. * XXXX, 2003 - Left for the U.S., after XXXX, 2003 attack by 2 motorcyclists shooting at his car. He said his parents in Bogota received threatening calls directed at him.

The foregoing indicates that the principal claimant left for the U.S. 4 times after having received threats from the FARC and returned 3 times despite that. In-between, he left 1 time and returned 1 time with no indication of threats received.

The Panel does not find the claimants to be Convention refugees or persons in need of protection as the Panel does not find the principal claimant's story to be wholly credible as to its crucial aspects. Alternatively, the Panel finds there is adequate state protection for them in Colombia today. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimants' identities were established by certified copies of their country passports and other identification documents as tendered into evidence.3 Nexus
As the Panel does not believe that the principal claimant was or is a target of the FARC, the Panel does not find there to be a nexus to any of the Convention grounds in this case Credibility
The determinative issue in this case is credibility. The Panel does not find the principal claimant's story, in respect to his fear, credible based on the following:

The Panel notes that the principal claimant allegedly fled to the U.S. 4 times (including the last one) and then returning to Bogota 3 times despite having been threatened by the FARC. After the first reavailment, he said he left for the U.S. in XXXX 2000 and returned shortly thereafter, but that this was under no threat by the FARC. The claimant alleged his reasons for return included the fact he was young, no more threats were received at those times and he wanted to finish his studies in Bogota.

Considering the number of times he left and returned, despite having been threatened, and despite his alleged reasons for returning, the Panel finds it hard to believe the existence of his subjective fear or even that he was threatened by the FARC. It does not stand to reason that he would, if his story of being a target of the FARC were true, keep on returning to Bogota between 3 to 6 months after supposedly fleeing the country. On this basis, leaving little to no weight to the denunciation he said was filed against the FARC or the genuineness of the letter he allegedly received from the FARC, the Panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that he was not or is not a target of the FARC.

Furthermore, the Panel notes that his parents continue to live in Bogota at a location known to the FARC but have not been confronted by the FARC or received any reprisal for their son's allegedly having offended them by his work as a process server, by the denunciation filed against the FARC or by the son having eluded them. The Panel adds this note as a further point against the credibility of his allegation that he was or is a target of the FARC.

Furthermore, he said that shortly after the attack by the 2 motorcycle men on XXXX, 2003, he and his parents had filed a denunciation with police naming the FARC as the attackers. They did not follow-up. He simply left for the U.S. on XXXX, 2003. The Panel draws a negative inference from this apparent window-dressing to his claim in that he would not have been present to testify on this denunciation, if indeed he had filed the complaint, and if the police decided to proceed on the case. The only reason the Panel can, therefore, see in alleging that he and/or his parents had filed a denunciation was to make it appear his story, that he was being targeted by the FARC, was true. From this, the Panel, therefore, further believes that, on a balance of probabilities, his allegation of being a target of the FARC is not true. State Protection
As an alternative to credibility, state protection is a determinative issue.

While states are presumed to be capable of protecting their nationals, it was open to the principal claimant, according to the law, to rebut the presumption of protection with clear and convincing evidence that adequate protection would not reasonably be forthcoming. The Panel finds, on the evidence, that the principal claimant has not rebutted that presumption and, therefore, these claims fail.

He said he and his parents had filed a denunciation naming the FARC for the attack. However, they did not do any follow-up on this complaint as he said they feared reprisal from the FARC. However, aside from the fact the Panel does not find this reason for not doing a follow-up not make sense since the FARC could have exacted reprisal on them for simply filing the denunciation, the Panel notes the principal claimant did not seek the assistance of other government law enforcement agencies, e.g. the GAULA (Unified Action Groups for Personal Freedom, a multi-force task group against terrorist and criminal organizations, formed in 1996). The Panel notes that there were and are law enforcement agencies especially established to deal with the FARC and FARC-related problems of Colombians, and that most of their personnel are not corrupt. The Panel also refers to the DAS (Administrative Security Department, similar to the F.B.I. of the U.S.A., formed in 1960). If indeed his problems with the FARC were true, he could have gone to these agencies for assistance, a reasonable step to take, beyond his denunciation with local police, as these are the agencies responsible for counter-actions and complaints against terrorist groups, i.e. the FARC. These law enforcement agencies have been documented to have had significant positive results since they were organized.4

Colombia is a working democracy with the state apparatus to provide adequate protection to its citizens. The principal claimant's inaction at not taking any reasonable step to file complaints with or seek the help of responsible government agencies is not reflective of the state's inability or unwillingness to provide adequate state protection.

Canadian jurisprudence states the following: * States are presumed to be capable of protecting their citizens, except in situations where the state is in a state of complete breakdown. (Ward.)5 * The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. (Ward.)6 * The presumption of state protection applies equally to cases where the state (or an agent of state) is alleged to be a persecutor. (Hinzman.)7 * To rebut the presumption of state protection, the burden is on the principal claimant to provide "clear and convincing" evidence of the state's inability to protect its citizens, (absent an admission by the national's state of its inability to protect that national). (Ward.)8 A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that the evidence establishes that state protection is inadequate (Flores Carrillo).9 The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate. (Flores Carrillo.)10 * Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the state's efforts are not always successful does not rebut the presumption of state protection. (Villafranca.)11 * A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state (Judge,12 Camacho).13 Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection. (Rio Ramirez.)14

The following is a summary of the current state of affairs on adequacy of state protection and the state's efforts to provide its citizens with state protection from terrorist groups, such as the FARC and the ELN (National Liberation Army). (Because of the close relationship between the FARC and the ELN and similarities in ideology and purpose, this discussion in referring to the FARC to a certain extent refers to the ELN, as well. Both groups are called collectively as the "guerrillas.")

The Panel has respectfully taken into consideration counsel's closing submissions and news articles and reports tendered into evidence, some of which basically suggest that guerrilla activity in the country is far from over. In that respect, the Panel takes note of the following. The findings in this paragraph and the next paragraphs attempt to provide a balanced view of the situation and are supported by specific references to the documentary evidence following this analysis.

The FARC has existed for more than 40 years, initially as a communist movement to protect the interests of Colombian peasants from the perceived excesses of the rich and powerful. Over the past decade and more, the FARC has become essentially a narco-terrorist group and appears to be devoid of its initial objectives i.e., to help the poor in the rural areas. In fact, these poor rural people are abused, targeted and victimized more and more by the FARC. The previous government of President Uribe was installed in August 2002 on the promise of serious commitments to fight and disarm the FARC. He delivered on these by dramatically increasing resources given to army and police and other state instruments. The FARC still exists but its strength has been severely reduced due to persistent government efforts including substantial material and logistical help from Western powers, particularly the U.S.A. The FARC has shown some degree of resilience despite the setbacks of the past 8 years caused by persistent and escalating government efforts against it, but its capability of surviving these is currently the subject of much speculation dependent on how well it taps its new found focus on the drug trade vis a vis a determined government shored up by military successes that appear to be recently intensifying and escalating, with the support of the U.S. and other Western powers and almost total support by its population weary of the FARC-problem.

Documentary evidence, reflected in some articles and reports, do not always provide a precise picture of the current state of the FARC, mainly because there are too many interest groups painting somewhat conflicting pictures of the FARC, its strength and capabilities. However, objective evidence does question the current capacity of the FARC to harm civilians at will and to effectively communicate among its own leadership. Furthermore, most of the surviving leaders are hiding in deeply forested mountains along and outside the national boundaries. The state of Colombia has in fact gone beyond her national boundaries and apprehended or killed FARC leaders and destroyed their camps in adjoining countries, even creating diplomatic tiffs with Ecuador and Venezuela. Documentary evidence shows that the FARC still targets high-profile politicians, major human rights defenders and senior members of the army, police and judiciary in certain parts of the country. They took credit for the kidnapping of a Governor of a department and killing him. Documentary evidence does not, however, support the point that the FARC is targeting people for petty extortion and or keeping track of them all over this vast country.

The current government of President Santos, which was elected on the promise of continuing the assault on the FARC, is stepping up its efforts against the FARC and achieving successes in demolishing the organization's leadership and structures. Colombia a democratic state

Documentary evidence15 that the Panel views, on a balance of probabilities, as reliable clearly shows that Colombia is a functioning democracy where civilians have recourse to the state apparatus, i.e., security forces and police, when they require protection from criminal acts and human rights abuses and persecution. Those accused of such acts are held accountable for their actions through the rule of law. Elections were generally considered fair and free and took place in an atmosphere of freedom, transparency and normalcy.16 Moreover, * Civilian authorities generally maintained control of multi-level security forces consisting of local, national police forces and a national army.17 * The National Police are responsible for internal law enforcement, shared with the Department of Administrative Security (DAS) and the Prosecutor General's Corps of Technical Investigators (CTI).18 Europa World Year Book 200919

Furthermore, * Uribe resolved and delivered resources "...to strenghten the capacity of the government to achieve a lasting victory over the rebel groups. ...Issued a decree establishing a 'state of internal disturbance' and introducing a war tax... extended police powers, ...pledged to double the size of the army ...recruit a further 100,000 police officers". "In December 2003, the Congresso approved a series of antiterrorism measures, granting extensive powers to police and military" (p1343). This also shows that the Uribe administration had in the past helped create paramilitary groups as an anti-FARC initiative, which was later found by the courts to be illegal, steering the government into resolving the problem by entering into a demobilization of these paramilitary groups in 2006. Several members of the Congresso and administration were prosecuted by the Supreme Court for involvement, thus showing a government determined at preserving the rule of law and upholding the independece of the Judiciary. * In April 2004, 17,000 troops were deployed in traditional FARC strongholds in a U.S.-funded Military campaign (p 1344) * "... Colombian armed forces launched a raid on a FARC training camp in Ecuador, killing 17 rebels, including the group's second-in-command.." FARC was further debilitated later in that month by the death... of its commander-in-chief.... (p 1344) * The government secured a major victory when special forces rescued the group's highest-profile hostage (p 1344). US DOS report20

Furthermore, * Guerilla group members continue to demobilize. In 2009, 2,481 guerillas demobilized compared with 3,420 in 2008. In addition indigenous groups are also leaving these groups and joining the reserves. * "FARC and ELN guerillas killed journalists, religious leaders, candidates for political office, local elected officials and polticians, alleged paramilitary collaborators and members of government security forces." FARC-ELN alliances remained to be fragile - the FARC's 8,000 to 9,000 members and the ELN's 2,000 members worked together in some parts of the country and fought against each other in other parts. In 11 months of the year, the FARC killed 220 civilians. The FARC threatened and harassed doctors and nurses. * However, political parties operate without restrictions or outside interference. * Government officials have been forced to resign, were prosecuted and incarcerated for corruption and abuse of authority. The Supreme Court, with support and funding from the President, continues its investigation of Congreso members and senior government officials. Despite advances in the Justice and Peace Law process, the application of the law continues to face some problems. UNHCR Refugee Eligibility Guidelines21

Furthermore, * "Since 2003, President Alvaro Uribe committed to defeat the guerrillas pursuant to the 'Democratic Security and Defence Policy'. The current military efforts, such as the killing of FARC's chief commanders and the dismantling of its military structure, have significantly weakened the FARC....The Colombian Government reports that in 2009, almost 2,700 guerrilla members were demobilized." (p 4). This highly respected source also lists 11 groups that are targeted by the FARC, similar to the target identified by the U.S. DOS earlier. Noteworthy is that there is no reference to the FARC targeting people for their failure to pay the demanded extortion. Amnesty International22

This report indicates that * There was a rise in killings of members of marginalized social groups and indigenous people," who typically live in remote regions of Colombia where the FARC is present. * The number of kidnappings fell to 213 in 2009 from 437 in 2008. Most kidnappings were attributed to criminal gangs rather than the FARC or ELN (p 110). UNITED NATIONS HIGH COMMISSIONER FOR HUMAN RIGHTS23 * Para. 29. The FARC-EP continued indiscriminate attacks, seriously affecting the civilian population, such as the launching of explosives, which killed 3 individuals in Corinto (Cauca) in May 2008; acts of terrorism, such as the attacks on the Cali Palace of Justice (Valle del Cauca), which resulted in the death of 4 persons and wounding 26, in September 2008, and the one in the village of Ituango (Antioquia) in August 2008, in which 55 persons were injured and 7, including one child, died. * Para. 30. Increased planting of anti-personnel mines by guerrilla groups has caused a high number of civilian and military casualties, among them children. * Para. 57. Judicial processes constitute a positive step in the struggle against impunity and the strengthening of the rule of law, which needs to be preserved and shielded from any politicization. * Para. 63. Previous reports of the High Commissioner highlighted the need to guarantee the rights of all victims and the importance of placing them at the centre of relevant public debates. In 2008, the plight of victims and their rights gained momentum within the political and public agendas. Among the victims, women have faced the most obstacles and stigmatization..." * Para. 66. The judiciary has also paid special attention to the rights of victims. In various decisions, courts have, for example, confirmed the right of victims to participate in the "voluntary depositions" under the Justice and Peace Law; * Para. 67. Public accounts about the sufferings of those kidnapped by the FARC-EP and of families of victims of extrajudicial executions have generated a feeling of anti-FARC-EP solidarity across the Colombian society. The media has helped to create social awareness.... OPERATIONAL GUIDANCE NOTE, Colombia, UK Home Office24 * Para. 2.6 The Government's respect for human rights continued to improve in 2007. Government steps to improve the human rights and security situation in Colombia showed demonstrable results during the year and government statistics indicated that there were decreases in massacres (34 %) and kidnappings (29 %). * Para. 2.7. Some serious problems remain, however, and in 2007 there were reports that elements of the security forces continued to collaborate with paramilitary groups, who refused to demobilize, who were responsible for serious human rights abuses and who had degenerated into renegade criminal groups more intent on the drug trade. * Para. 2.8. The Justice and Peace Law (LJP) process has exposed corruption and paramilitary ties within the Government and the security forces. In 2007, President Uribe urged the Supreme Court to punish public officials found guilty and continued funding of the Supreme Court's Investigative Unit, which investigates members of Congress and senior government officials. During the year, investigations by the Supreme Court and Prosecutor General's Office of links between politicians and paramilitary groups implicated 52 congressmen, 11 governors, and 19 mayors; 18 congressmen, 14 mayors, and 2 governors were in jail at year's end. * Para. 3.6.4. In 2007, the FARC and ELN reportedly continued to commit human rights abuses, including political killings; killings of off-duty members of the public security forces and local officials.... * Para. 3.6.5. Sufficiency of protection - The state authorities are willing to offer protection to such individuals, however their capacity to actually provide it is limited due to the Government's weak authority in some regions and inability to counter the influence in parts of the country of the FARC, ELN, and paramilitaries who refuse to demobilize. While the new illegal groups lack the organization, reach and military capacity of the former AUC (United Self Defense Forces of Colombia, paramilitaries), guerrilla organizations continue to operate nationwide and are well-resourced to dominate some areas in which they see a particular interest. The state therefore cannot currently always offer sufficient protection from these groups. (It should be noted that the inadequacy of protection refers to persons outlined in para. 3.6.4 above and not ordinary victims of attempted extortion, and the report is dated 2008 and thus may represent data for the years prior). International Crisis Group April 28, 200825 * Almost 6 years of intense security operations against the FARC by the administration of President Álvaro Uribe are beginning to produce tangible results. Government forces killed several important rebel field commanders in 2007 and 2 members of the central command in March 2008, including second-in-command Raúl Reyes, and have severely disrupted insurgent communications, prompting a loss of internal cohesion and decreasing illegal revenues (page 1). * The national political climate has reinforced the government's stance. On 4 February 2008, over 4 million people marched against the FARC. The rejection of the FARC by the general population has been recognized by all political forces. An important faction of the left-wing Polo Democratico Alternativo (PDA) party has denounced the FARC's inhumane practices and clearly distanced itself from the insurgency, which it does not recognize as a legitimate left-wing force (page 2). * Recent successful military strikes against the FARC leadership and other signs of rebel weakness have led government and security force officials to claim Colombia was nearing "the end of the end" of the FARC. The government states that it intends to continue and even increase the military pressure so as to force the FARC to the negotiating table. It also asserts a willingness to use the Justice and Peace Law as the legal framework for removing the FARC from the battlefield, which implies FARC leaders could expect to serve no more than 8 years in jail (page 7). * The FARC's once stable command structure is believed to be faltering. The death of Ríos at the hands of his own men is a clear reflection of the loss in internal cohesion. Moreover, security force sources say that the lack of internal communication due to military pressure and technical surveillance and the increasing demobilization of experienced mid-level commanders are also affecting the chain of command. As morale crumbles, government officials believe political and ideological fissures will widen within the FARC leadership, prompting power struggles which could lead the organization to slowly fracture or even implode (page 7). * According to security force sources, the FARC is also increasingly less operational. Government estimates show it going from more than 18,900 fighters in 2002 to between 9,000 and 11,000 in 2007, with only 10 of its 71 fronts and units regularly active (page 8)... There is reason to believe that the FARC is still capable to a degree of adapting and resisting, at least in the short to medium term (page 8). The situation of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia26 * The only source consulted that identifies the purpose of the kidnappings claimed by FARC is the Columbian online weekly Cambio, which states in a 28 November 2007 article that no ransom was demanded in 4 out of 11 kidnappings attributed to FARC in 2006. Instead, the kidnappers wanted to use the victim's business or bank accounts to launder money. * FARC's presence is felt primarily in the coca plantation regions in southeast Colombia (France2.fr 13 Dec. 2007). According to Cambio, the rebel group has withdrawn to the areas along the borders with Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama and its best fighters defend the territories where FARC is traditionally present - Guaviare and Caquetá departments, the southern part of Meta department, and Putumayo and Nariño departments. * According to Juan Manuel Santos, Colombia's Minister of Defence, FARC currently lacks means of communication (BBC 1 Feb. 2008). The BBC reports that "their radio and satellite communications are being intercepted thanks to U.S. technology" and that the organization has been forced to resort to using couriers (BBC 1 Feb. 2008). International Crisis Group 2009 report27 * The successes of the government's security strategy have resulted in part from the modernization and growth of its security forces, aided by substantial international technical and financial support, in particular from the U.S. Perhaps even more important have been improvements in the quality and quantity of strategic intelligence, which have enabled precision air raids to kill important rebel commanders and disrupt command-and control structures. * Key units of the FARC have withdrawn from the large urban centres to the jungle and mountains, and they now rely heavily on ambush attacks in those areas. * As with organized criminal groups, drug trafficking has gradually taken over the heart of the activities of the FARC and parts of the smaller ELN. * At the tactical level, structures have decentralized; however, some reports claim the Secretariat is still capable of co-ordinating actions around the country. * However, even though FARC is believed to have replaced its leaders in its senior command, co-ordination between senior and mid-ranking commanders remains to be difficult. * After pushing FARC out of heavily populated areas and regaining control of road arteries, ... the secuity forces are focusing on attacking traditional FARC strongholds. * Areas where FARC is strong and active are noted - western Meta, Purumayo, high mountain ranges or tropical jungle. (None of these include large urban populations centres.) * Security forces fear FARC will attempt to win back status in urban areas through selective terrorism but this is being heavily countered by state security forces with superior intelligence gathering and monitoring. Police have seized caches of explosives in the outskirts and FARC commandos have been arrested when attempting to penetrate cities. The first two complete paragraphs of page 12 indicate FARC urban units have been disrupted and dismantled rendering most ineffective; however, insurgents are known to remain active in Cali and Bueneventura. Now FARC works in independent cells as support networks have been progressivly weakened. In the early 2000's, urban fronts were driven out of cities like Bogota, Medellin, Cali and Cucuta. Security forces have made logistics vulnerable to interception and exert tight control via checkpoints on roads and rivers that lead from combat areas. * Extortion may have increased but is still under-reported. Individuals and common criminal gangs are suspected of using FARC's name as a mean to extract extortion. * Drug revenues have dropped from one billion to 500-600 million per year. * Increasing FARC defections make it easier for the government to collect intelligence. Ex-FARC fighters are interrogated at the defense ministry - "sucked dry of information," a U.S. embassy official said - before being sent to the presidency's high counsellor for reinsertion (Alta Consejería para la Reinserción, ACR). Based on information extracted from them, interception and infiltration of FARC units has increased dramatically. Demobilized combatants are also instrumental in encouraging former comrades to defect. Increasingly, defection of mid-ranking and senior commanders with over ten years in the FARC helps to convince those previously under their command to desert. * After pushing the FARC out of heavily populated areas and regaining control of road arteries and other strategic infrastructure, the security forces are focusing on attacking traditional FARC strongholds. * In urban areas, where three out of four Colombians live, FARC support has virtually vanished due to public opposition to the organization's preference of armed struggle over political action and the government's success in depicting it as the main security threat to Colombian society. * By contrast, the FARC reportedly continues to exert control over and carry out indoctrination of inhabitants of the remote and poor areas of Chocó, Meta, Norte de Santander, Antioquia, Guajira and Santander departments, as well as the coffee belt region (Quindío, Caldas and Risaralda departments). Political handbook of the World 201028 * Fueled by proceeds from its drug trade, FARC grew rapidly during the 1990s reaching approximately 18,000 members by the 2000s. * This report also shows that Colombia is a functioning democracy with a bi-cameral parliament and universal suffrage. International Narcotics Control Strategy 2010 for Colombia29 * Record coca eradication in 2008 resulted in significant decline in cocaine production potential and coca cultivation. * Pure cocaine production dropped by 39 percent from 485 metric tons in 2007 to 295 metric tons in 2008 compared with 700 metric tons in 2001. It is noted that FARC's area of control are primarily coca producing remote forests and even these are under constant attack and eradication. * High-Value Targets (HVTs). Because of the FARC's growing prominence in the drug trade, over 60 FARC leaders have been indicted since 2005 in the U.S. for conspiring to traffic cocaine into the U.S. After achieving a number of high-level and significant victories against the FARC in 2008, the government maintained pressure against the terrorist organization and succeeded in capturing or killing a number of high-level FARC commanders in 2009. Under "Operation Fuerte," Colombian forces killed the commander and captured the deputy commander of the FARC's "Antonio Narino" urban front. On May 30, Colombian police captured Adela Perez, a senior FARC leader who participated in the 1994 car bomb assassination of a Colombian general and a 2001 assassination attempt against Colombian President Alvaro Uribe. * The government's National Directorate for Dangerous Drugs (DNE) reported that Colombian security forces seized a total of 205.85 metric tons of cocaine and cocaine base, 191.6 metric tons of marijuana, 740 kilograms of heroin, over 1.35 million gallons and 3.54 million kilograms of precursor chemicals, while destroying 285 cocaine hydrochloride (HCL) labs and 2,795 coca base labs during 2009. Kidnappings and extortion30 * The key perpetrators of the kidnappings for extortion were, on the one hand, the FARC (62 cases) and the ELN (39 cases), and, on the other hand, small-scale criminals (91 cases) (ibid.). Of these, the small-scale criminal cases basically represent almost half of the total. * The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) indicates that the kidnappings, with or without extortion, took place primarily in rural areas and that "businessmen and public figures are targets ... [for] guerrillas and common criminals" (20 Nov. 2006). Crime in Colombia31 * In Colombia's 6 largest cities, the most common crimes are theft without violence (73 percent) and armed robbery in the street (20 percent) (ibid., 6). [Not FARC terrorist actions]. According to the study in Bogotá. * In 2008, 45 percent of people who stated that they were the victim of a crime reported the crime, compared with only 17.6 percent in 2007 and 40 percent in 2006; * The police registered most of the complaints (87 percent), followed by the Office of the Attorney General (Fiscalía General de la Nación) (13 percent); * 39 percent of participants felt that the police are doing a good job. Update on the FARC Situation

Although, the recent International Crisis Group report of 29 June 201032 recognizes security problems the country is wrestling with, there are indications of overall significant gains in this regard, notably as follows: * Page 1 - The government's campaign against the FARC "has taken a heavy toll on Colombia's largest insurgent organization. The government is now working to consolidate security gains by expanding state presence in several of the formerly most conflict-ridden regions" and the FARC as an organization "has lost thousands of fighters due to deaths in combat, captures and desertions...." * Page 2 - The research indicates that "across Colombia (Bogota, Antioquia, Narino, Choco, Norte de Santander, Meta and Sucre departments)... in 2010 FARC's military capacity is strongly reduced and the organization is experiencing serious coordination and communication problems." It said further that "in 2010, the guerrilla organization is estimated to have around 8,000-10,000 combatants, organized in 61 fronts (frentes), of which only 30 are believed to be active..." * Page 3 - "High levels of desertion have weakened the FARC and lowered morale among its rank and file." "Particularly problematic for FARC has been the increasing loss, especially since 2008, of mid-ranking commanders with a long record in the organization." This loss is considered acute because these commanders "tend to be responsible for maintaining discipline and morale among the troops and establishing relationships with local populations." "FARC has been unable to capitalize on the string of unilateral and unconditional releases of mostly civilian hostages it has carried out since early 2008." "FARC's diminished capacity and capability is forcing it to avoid large scale confrontations with government forces..." * Page 4 - "As of April 2010, the police had confiscated 1,663 rifles" and "6,000 arms were confiscated in the previous two years." * Page 5 - "FARC has lost most of its support among the population." * Page 7 - "Uribe's military offensive has increasingly denied the insurgents sources of income, particularly from kidnappings for ransom" forcing the guerrillas to shift their attention to the drug trade, putting into spotlight the change in the character of the organization as a radical political force to that of a criminal gang. * Page 15 - The report concludes that while the FARC has not been completely defeated, it has been significantly weakened due to the government's military successes.

3 recent newspaper articles,33 talk about the "coup de grace" the current Santos administration has dealt on the FARC with the recent killing by the military of Mono Jojoy, "the military strategist and top commander of the organization" and Commander Domingo Biojo, political leader of the FARC's 48th Front. These along with the 2008 deaths of FARC founder Manuel Marulanda and secretariat member Alape are looked upon as the continuation of the end of the FARC as an effective rebel organization in Colombia. Intelligence data seized from the FARC camps and from defectors has made it possible to even locate FARC members hiding across the border in Venezuela. The treasure trove of data seized from the recent raid on Mono Jojoy's camp is expected to yield more information contributing to the demise of the FARC. The first article states that "FARC is now unable to operate effectively within national borders. No terrorist guerrilla has ever won a war in exile." The fourth article is a whole front-page from the Travel Section of the Toronto Star, Saturday, February 12, 2011, with the headline "Bogota Rolling with Optimism," and caption - "Colombia's capital transforms into a destination for good times and great art," touting Colombia as a great place to visit with the FARC problem greatly diminished and the country, particularly Bogota the capital city, made more secure by Uribe's government, a program continued by the current Santos regime.

Articles and reports submitted by counsel and/or the claimant indicate a continuing FARC activity, which the above discussion recognizes. However, it is noted that government counter-action has been increasingly successful and decisive and the FARC is losing or has lost most of its key and powerful leaders, putting its central command apparatus in disarray and its activities much more subdued and isolated. Summation of this analysis on state protection

State protection in the country is not perfect, but the foregoing analysis shows that, on the balance, the state is responding to the needs of its citizens. It has resources and it has been and continues to be increasingly effective. Corruption and impunity have been issues but these are being addressed and supported at the highest levels and the independent judiciary is using and expanding powers to prosecute not only the parliamentarians but also senior civil servants and security personnel.

The FARC, and to a similar extent the ELN, has shown a degree of resilience and still manages to operate but its sphere of influence is getting smaller and the fragmented organization's manpower has been reduced and relegated mostly to some remote rural and border mountain areas, and more so away from the major urban centres, i.e. Bogota. There are the occasional terrorist incidents in the cities, but the defense forces have been achieving tangible results against the guerrillas with significant backing by the U.S. and other western governments. Based on the foregoing, the Panel finds that the state of Colombia is able to provide adequate, if not perfect, protection for its citizens. The Canadian courts have stated that the test for a finding of state protection is whether that state protection is adequate.34 The Panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the state of Colombia is able to provide adequate state protection to the claimants.

Based on the foregoing, the Panel finds that the principal claimant has not discharged his onus of rebutting the presumption of protection available to him and his wife if they were to return to Colombia today. Is the Principal Claimant Still a Target of the FARC Today?
At this point, the Panel adds this section as an addendum to the discussion on Credibility vis a vis the analysis on State Protection:

With FARC's significantly diminished capacity, territory, fragmentation and destroyed central command, the Panel does not believe, on a balance of probabilities, that the principal claimant would still be in FARC data banks of military targets, even if he had been so when he left Colombia for the last time 8 years ago. It is also reasonable to doubt such data banks as the FARC may have had in 2003 would still be intact or exist today considering the successful government strikes against FARC personnel and facilities.

Furthermore, based on the principal claimant's story, he was merely a XXXX XXXX or XXXX XXXX XXXX, a fact that would have been obvious to the imprisoned FARC man in XXXX 2000. He had apparently left that job in XXXX 2000 when he left for the U.S. that is 11 years ago. It is, therefore, reasonable to assume that with his relatively low profile and the fact he had left the court clerk job, the FARC would turn their attention to more pressing matters or more high profile targets. The Panel is, therefore, not persuaded to believe that he is, if he had once been, a person of interest to the FARC today.

Having taken all the evidence into account, including counsel's submissions, I find that the claimants do not face a serious possibility of persecution or harm if they were to return to Colombia today. Furthermore, the Panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that they do not face a danger of torture or risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment were they to return to their country of origin.
Taking into consideration the foregoing, the Panel does not find it necessary to cover any further issues on this case.

The Refugee Protection Division, therefore, determines that the claimants are neither Convention refugees within the meaning of section 96 of the IRPA nor persons in need of protection under subsection 97(1). Their claims are, therefore, rejected. (signed) "W. Lim" W.
